title: Fast Food Poisoning, Colourless MacConkey Colonies, Salmonella Serotypes and H. pylori Tests
summary: Separate preformed-toxin food poisoning (S. aureus, emetic B. cereus) from the slower diarrhoeal B. cereus form, treat a colourless MacConkey colony from bloody stool as a suspect rather than a diagnosis, and learn what Salmonella serotyping and the H. pylori tests actually detect.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 57 Hit 16 (staphylococcal and B. cereus food poisoning timing), Hit 25 (non-lactose-fermenting MacConkey colonies + bloody diarrhoea = Shigella) and Hit 41 (Salmonella serotyping; H. pylori tests). Checked against Argudín 2010, Kadariya 2014, Dietrich 2021, the IDSA 2017 diarrhoea guideline (Shane; read via a page-fetch tool, first part of the page only), Ud-Din 2014, Kröger 2023, Tickell 2017, Ibrahim 2018, Diep 2019, the Irish H. pylori consensus (Smith 2024), Dore 2021 and Ali 2024. Corrections: staphylococcal onset is given as 2–8 h (usually 3–5 h), not 1–6 h (rv-staph-food-onset); a colourless colony plus bloody stool is not specific for Shigella (rv-nlf-bloody-not-shigella); serotype alone does not establish an outbreak link (rv-salmonella-serotype-outbreak); H. pylori stool antigen is an immunoassay and test preparation matters (rv-hpylori-test-context). The Maastricht VI/Florence consensus was not read (not open in PMC). Not taught: B. cereus quantitative food culture threshold, Vi antigen, H. pylori treatment.

objectives: Contrast preformed-toxin food poisoning (S. aureus, emetic B. cereus) with the diarrhoeal B. cereus form by onset, symptoms and toxin heat stability.
Explain why a colourless MacConkey colony from bloody stool needs full identification before Shigella is reported.
State the antigens used in Salmonella serotyping and its limits for outbreak linkage.
Match each H. pylori test to what it detects and state the drug-washout rules before testing.

scenes.title: Three gut puzzles
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three gut cases arrive on one shift — (1) a lunch group vomiting a few hours after a reheated rice dish; (2) a stool from a patient with bloody diarrhoea growing colourless colonies on MacConkey agar; (3) a patient taking a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) who is booked for a Helicobacter pylori urea breath test tomorrow. Question token: “Which toxin, which organism, which test?”

cues.text: Three gut puzzles arrive on one shift. A lunch group is vomiting a few hours after eating a reheated rice dish.
A stool from a patient with bloody diarrhoea grows colourless colonies on MacConkey agar. And a patient taking a proton pump inhibitor is booked for an H. pylori breath test tomorrow.
Which toxin, which organism, and is that test ready to run?

props.label: Which toxin, which organism, which test?

scenes.title: Toxin in the food vs toxin made in the gut
scenes.altText: Three cards. Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning: enterotoxins are preformed in the food, resist heat, low pH and proteolytic enzymes; rapid onset (2–8 h in one review; usually 3–5 h in another) of nausea and violent vomiting, with or without diarrhoea; usually resolves within 24–48 h. Bacillus cereus emetic form: the toxin cereulide is preformed in the food and is extremely stable to heat, acid and digestive enzymes; vomiting 15 min to 6 h after eating; historically linked to starchy foods such as rice and pasta. B. cereus diarrhoeal form: viable cells or spores must be eaten and make enterotoxins in the intestine (toxins preformed in food are sensitive to heat, acid and proteases); diarrhoea and cramps after about 8–16 h.

cues.text: Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning is caused by enterotoxin already made in the food. The toxin survives heat, stomach acid and digestive enzymes.
Symptoms start fast, within about two to eight hours, often three to five: nausea and violent vomiting, with or without diarrhoea. Most patients recover within one to two days.

Bacillus cereus has an emetic form that looks the same. Its toxin, cereulide, is also made in the food and is extremely heat-stable. Vomiting starts fifteen minutes to six hours after eating; it was historically linked to rice and pasta.
The diarrhoeal form is different. Live cells or spores are eaten and make enterotoxin inside the gut, so diarrhoea and cramps start later, after about eight to sixteen hours.

props.title: B. cereus diarrhoeal
lines: Enterotoxin made in the gut by live cells

scenes.title: A colourless colony is a suspect, not a verdict
scenes.altText: MacConkey card: colourless (lactose-negative) colonies. Shigella card: usually lactose-negative, non-motile, lysine-decarboxylase-negative; Shigella sonnei can ferment lactose slowly. Look-alike card: many enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) strains share these traits and causes dysentery by the same invasion mechanism; Salmonella enterica typically cannot metabolise lactose (rare lactose-fermenting strains exist). Bloody-stool card (IDSA 2017 table): STEC, Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Entamoeba histolytica, non-cholera Vibrio, Yersinia and others. A systematic review found dysentery identified only 1.9–85.9% of confirmed Shigella infections. Hook answer 2: suspect Shigella, then complete identification.

cues.text: Now the colourless colonies. On MacConkey agar, colourless means the organism did not ferment lactose. Shigella is the classic example: usually lactose-negative, non-motile, and lysine-decarboxylase-negative.

But it is not the only one. Shigella sonnei can ferment lactose slowly. Many enteroinvasive E. coli strains share Shigella’s traits and cause the same kind of dysentery. Salmonella usually cannot use lactose either.

And bloody stool has a long list of causes: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Entamoeba histolytica, Yersinia and more. Many Shigella infections are not bloody at all.
So for the second case, the colourless colony is a suspect, not a verdict. Finish the identification before reporting Shigella.

scenes.title: Serotyping Salmonella and finding H. pylori
scenes.altText: Salmonella card: serotype by agglutination with antisera against somatic O (lipopolysaccharide) and flagellar H antigens, read against the Kauffmann-White (White-Kauffmann-Le Minor) scheme; about 2,600 serovars recognised (2011 count); serotyping is the first-line characterisation for surveillance but is not discriminatory enough on its own for outbreak investigation, so molecular subtyping and whole-genome sequencing are added. H. pylori card: urease splits urea to ammonia and carbon dioxide — urea breath test (13C-labelled urea), rapid urease test on biopsy (pH indicator); monoclonal stool antigen is an immunoassay; serology cannot separate active from past infection. Prep card (Irish consensus 2024): stop PPIs 14 days before testing (unless PCR is used); avoid antibiotics and bismuth for 4 weeks. Hook answer 3: postpone the breath test.

cues.text: Salmonella serotyping uses antisera. Somatic O antigens, from the lipopolysaccharide, and flagellar H antigens are matched to the Kauffmann-White scheme, now called White-Kauffmann-Le Minor. About two thousand six hundred serovars are recognised.
Serotype is the first step in public health surveillance, but on its own it cannot prove two cases are linked. Outbreak work adds molecular subtyping and whole-genome sequencing.

Helicobacter pylori makes urease, which turns urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. The breath test detects labelled carbon dioxide, and the rapid urease test on a biopsy detects the alkaline ammonia. The stool antigen test is an immunoassay, and serology cannot separate active from past infection.
Proton pump inhibitors lower test accuracy. One national consensus says stop them fourteen days before testing, and antibiotics or bismuth four weeks before. So the third patient’s test should wait.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Reheating the food destroys the toxin” (✓ S. aureus enterotoxins and cereulide are heat-stable); “Colourless MacConkey colony + bloody stool = report Shigella” (✓ EIEC and Salmonella are often lactose-negative too; finish identification); “Same Salmonella serotype = same outbreak” (✓ serotype is first-line; linking cases needs molecular subtyping or whole-genome sequencing).

cues.text: Trap one: reheating the food destroys the toxin. No: staphylococcal enterotoxins and cereulide survive heat.
Trap two: a colourless MacConkey colony from bloody stool means Shigella. No: enteroinvasive E. coli and Salmonella are often lactose-negative too. Finish the identification.
Trap three: the same Salmonella serotype proves the same outbreak. No: serotype is the first step; linking cases needs molecular subtyping.

scenes.title: Made in the dish, or made in the gut?
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Made in the DISH = fast vomit; made in the GUT = slow diarrhoea.” Tokens: dish = S. aureus, emetic B. cereus · gut = diarrhoeal B. cereus. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: made in the dish means fast vomiting, as with staphylococcal enterotoxin and cereulide. Made in the gut means slow diarrhoea, as with the diarrhoeal form of Bacillus cereus.

Where it breaks: onset depends on how much toxin was eaten, so the time windows overlap; staphylococcal poisoning can cause diarrhoea too; and emetic Bacillus cereus is found in many foods besides rice.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Toxin made in the food → vomiting within hours; made in the gut → diarrhoea later”, “Colourless colony = suspect · serotype = O + H · stop PPI before H. pylori tests”.

cues.text: Preformed heat-stable toxins from Staphylococcus aureus and emetic Bacillus cereus cause vomiting within hours, a colourless MacConkey colony from bloody stool is a suspect that still needs full identification, Salmonella serotypes come from O and H antigens, and Helicobacter pylori tests need proton pump inhibitors stopped first.

props.label: Toxin in food → fast vomiting · made in gut → slow diarrhoea
Colourless = suspect · serotype = O + H · stop PPI first

explanation.what: Plain language: some food poisoning comes from toxin already sitting in the food, so people vomit within hours; other forms need live bacteria to make toxin in the gut, so symptoms come later. A colourless colony on MacConkey only says the organism does not use lactose; several gut pathogens look like that. Salmonella strains are named by the antigens on their surface and flagella. H. pylori is found by its urease or by its antigens, and proton pump inhibitors, antibiotics and bismuth can hide it. Scientific terms: staphylococcal enterotoxin, cereulide, emetic and diarrhoeal syndromes, lactose fermentation, lysine decarboxylase, enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC), somatic O and flagellar H antigens, White-Kauffmann-Le Minor scheme, whole-genome sequencing (WGS), urea breath test, rapid urease test, monoclonal stool antigen test, serology.
explanation.why: Preformed toxins act without bacterial growth in the host, so onset is short; staphylococcal enterotoxins and cereulide resist heat, acid and proteases, so reheating food does not make it safe. Lactose fermentation is a broad screen, not a species marker. Serotyping groups isolates but is not discriminatory enough to link cases. Urease lets H. pylori survive gastric acid and is the basis of two tests; PPIs, antibiotics and bismuth lower the bacterial load and can cause false negatives.
explanation.measure: Onset: S. aureus about 2–8 h (usually 3–5 h), recovery in 24–48 h; emetic B. cereus 15 min–6 h; diarrhoeal B. cereus about 8–16 h. Shigella: usually lactose-negative, non-motile, lysine-decarboxylase-negative; S. sonnei may ferment lactose slowly. Salmonella: O + H antigen agglutination; about 2,600 serovars. H. pylori (Irish consensus 2024): urea breath test preferred non-invasive test, monoclonal stool antigen as alternative; stop PPIs 14 days before testing (unless PCR is used); avoid antibiotics and bismuth for 4 weeks; serology not for confirming eradication.
explanation.differs: Preformed toxin (fast, vomiting) vs toxin made in the gut (slower, diarrhoea); Shigella vs EIEC vs Salmonella (all often lactose-negative); serotype (first-line grouping) vs molecular subtyping (case linkage); urease-based tests vs stool antigen immunoassay vs serology.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: match onset time and symptoms to the food-poisoning organism, pick the next step after colourless colonies from bloody stool, name the antigens in Salmonella serotyping, or choose the right H. pylori test and preparation.

mnemonic.text: Made in the DISH = fast vomit; made in the GUT = slow diarrhoea.
mnemonic.explanation: Preformed toxins (S. aureus enterotoxin, B. cereus cereulide) act within hours; the diarrhoeal B. cereus form needs live bacteria to make toxin in the intestine.
mnemonic.limitation: Onset depends on toxin dose and the windows overlap; staphylococcal poisoning can include diarrhoea; emetic B. cereus is found in many foods besides rice.

analogyLimitations: Onset ranges come from reviews and vary with toxin dose.
H. pylori preparation rules are from one national consensus (Ireland 2024); local guidance may differ.
takeaway: Preformed heat-stable toxins from Staphylococcus aureus and emetic Bacillus cereus cause vomiting within hours, a colourless MacConkey colony from bloody stool is a suspect that still needs full identification, Salmonella serotypes come from O and H antigens, and Helicobacter pylori tests need proton pump inhibitors stopped first.

questions.stem: Several people start vomiting about 2–4 hours after eating a reheated rice dish. Which explanation fits best?

options.text: Bacillus cereus emetic toxin (cereulide) preformed in the food
options.rationale: Correct. Cereulide is made in the food, is extremely heat-stable, and causes vomiting 15 min to 6 h after eating; rice and pasta are the classic foods.

options.text: Bacillus cereus enterotoxin made in the intestine after eating
options.rationale: Incorrect. The diarrhoeal form needs live cells to make toxin in the gut; it causes diarrhoea and cramps after about 8–16 h.

options.text: A heat-labile toxin, so reheating should have made the food safe
options.rationale: Incorrect. Cereulide and staphylococcal enterotoxins resist heat; reheating does not inactivate them.
Incorrect. STEC is a cause of bloody diarrhoea; vomiting within hours of a meal points to a preformed toxin (S. aureus or emetic B. cereus).

questions.stem: A stool from a patient with bloody diarrhoea grows colourless, non-motile, lysine-decarboxylase-negative colonies on MacConkey agar. What is the best next step?

options.text: Complete biochemical and serological identification before reporting Shigella
options.rationale: Correct. Shigella is suspected, but many enteroinvasive E. coli strains share these traits and other lactose-negative pathogens exist.

options.text: Report Shigella now: colourless colonies plus bloody stool are diagnostic
options.rationale: Incorrect. Lactose-negative growth is a screen, and bloody diarrhoea has many causes (STEC, Salmonella, Campylobacter and others).

options.text: Exclude Salmonella because Salmonella ferments lactose
options.rationale: Incorrect. Salmonella enterica typically cannot metabolise lactose; only rare strains do.

options.text: Exclude E. coli because all E. coli ferment lactose
options.rationale: Incorrect. Many enteroinvasive E. coli strains are lactose-negative and non-motile, like Shigella.

questions.stem: A patient taking a proton pump inhibitor daily is booked for an H. pylori urea breath test. According to the 2024 Irish consensus, what should happen first?

options.text: Stop the proton pump inhibitor 14 days before the test
options.rationale: Correct. PPIs reduce the accuracy of H. pylori tests, so they should be stopped 14 days before testing unless PCR is used.

options.text: Nothing; PPIs do not affect the breath test
options.rationale: Incorrect. PPIs lower the bacterial load and can cause false-negative results.

options.text: Switch to serology, which confirms active infection
options.rationale: Incorrect. Serology cannot distinguish active from past infection.

options.text: Switch to the stool antigen test, which measures urease activity
options.rationale: Incorrect. The stool antigen test is an immunoassay for H. pylori antigens, and PPIs affect it too.

claims.text: S. aureus onset ~2–8 h (usually 3–5 h), emetic B. cereus 15 min–6 h, diarrhoeal B. cereus ~8–16 h; short-incubation emetic syndrome.
Staphylococcal enterotoxins and cereulide preformed and heat/acid/protease-stable; diarrhoeal enterotoxins made in the gut.
Shigella lactose-negative, non-motile, LDC-negative; S. sonnei slow lactose; EIEC and Salmonella also lactose-negative; bloody stool has many causes; many Shigella infections are not dysenteric.
Salmonella serotyping by O and H antigen agglutination (Kauffmann-White / White-Kauffmann-Le Minor); ~2,600 serovars; first-line but insufficient alone for outbreak linkage.

H. pylori urease (acid survival) underlies UBT and rapid urease test; stool antigen is an immunoassay; serology cannot separate active from past infection; PPI 14-day and antibiotic/bismuth 4-week washout.
claims.note: Washout intervals are from the Irish 2024 consensus; local guidance may differ.

claims.text: “Made in the dish, made in the gut.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 57 Hit 16 gives staphylococcal food poisoning onset as 1–6 h. Argudín 2010 gives 2–8 h and Kadariya 2014 “usually 3–5 h”, depending on toxin dose; the lesson teaches about 2–8 h (register flag rv-staph-food-onset).

Ch. 57 Hit 25 equates colourless MacConkey colonies + bloody diarrhoea with Shigella. Many EIEC strains and most Salmonella are also lactose-negative, S. sonnei ferments lactose slowly, and IDSA 2017 lists many causes of bloody stool; the lesson teaches it as a presumptive finding needing identification (register flag rv-nlf-bloody-not-shigella).

Ch. 57 Hit 41 says serotype “drives outbreak tracking”. Ibrahim 2018 and Diep 2019 describe serotyping as the first-line characterisation that is not discriminatory enough on its own; outbreak linkage uses molecular subtyping/WGS. The scheme is now called White-Kauffmann-Le Minor (register flag rv-salmonella-serotype-outbreak).

Ch. 57 Hit 41 lists urea breath test, stool antigen and rapid urease test without noting that the stool antigen test is an immunoassay (not a urease test), that serology cannot separate active from past infection, and that PPIs/antibiotics/bismuth must be stopped before testing (Smith 2024; Dore 2021) (register flag rv-hpylori-test-context). Washout intervals are guideline-dependent.
